Subject: Capacity portfolio & ramp financing options — MedAlign

Hi Claire,

Thanks again for the conversation this morning — great to align on MedAlign's Q1 production needs. Per our ask list I pulled together three option sets that balance committed economics, warm-start safety, and a fast ramp path given your upcoming pilot and procurement window. The attached PDF has slides; below is a concise summary so you can circulate with procurement.

Option A — Baseline Commitment (Predictable, lowest unit cost)
- Cluster: 20 x H100-equivalent GPUs (dedicated pool)
- Minimum live allocation: 12 GPUs (60% active baseline)
- Ramp: 4 weeks activation to baseline, +8 weeks to full 20 GPUs
- Use case: steady inference with steady RPS and predictable seq length (<=1024)
- Commercial: 12-month commitment, monthly billing, unit token discount applied

Option B — Anchored Sprint (Fast scale + runway)
- Cluster: 50 x H100-equivalent GPUs (dedicated pool)
- Minimum live allocation: 10 GPUs (pilot lane) with burst to 50 via warm-pool
- Ramp: pilot (10 GPUs) immediate; scale to 50 within 6–10 weeks on committed schedule
- Use case: enterprise go-live with peak inference periods and sustained growth
- Commercial: 18-month commitment, staged ramp credits, amortized ramp fee option

Option C — Elastic Floor (Lower upfront, hybrid fallback)
- Cluster: 30 x A100/H100 mixed; software-enforced soft-floor = 8 GPUs
- Minimum live allocation: 8 GPUs guaranteed, additional capacity pulled on demand with prioritized routing
- Ramp: 6–12 week ramp depending on traffic evolution; includes burst credits for first 90 days
- Use case: uncertain traffic patterns, want lower committed spend but need reliability

Key notes across options:
- Warm-provisioning: We recommend pre-warm windows before known launch spikes; saves 20–35% on tail latency.
- Model variants: We'll route to quantized variants for background traffic to reduce cost without affecting critical flows.
- Sequence-length assumptions: pricing and core planning assume 1.2k token average; if your LLM usage skews >2k we should adjust sizing.

Attachments: [Attachment: MedAlign_Capacity_Portfolio_Q3.pdf (pdf)], [Attachment: MedAlign_pro-forma-costs.xlsx (xlsx)]

Next steps: If procurement prefers a lower capital entry, Option C + a 3-month pilot is easiest to sign. If product needs immediate headroom and predictable latency, Option B is the recommended path. Happy to align on a short call with procurement to walk the pro-forma.

Cheers,

Neha — thanks, this is helpful and concise. A couple of quick clarifying Qs from procurement and engineering:

1) For Option B, what's the committed minimum we can lock to avoid an immediate 50-GPU capex while still guaranteeing the scale path? Procurement prefers a smaller initial committed minimum if we can accept staged availability.
2) Are there SLAs tied to the minimum live allocation (e.g., latency P99 targets)? We need explicit language for our playbook.
3) On the mixed GPU proposal in Option C, can you confirm how instance selection (A100 vs H100) will be handled day-to-day — will Redwood route automatically based on model profile or is instance-type a manual config?

Procurement timeline: we're aiming to finalize commercial terms by 11/20 to align with our budget cycle.

Best,
Claire

Subject: Re: Capacity portfolio & ramp financing options — MedAlign

Great questions — answers inline below, and Karthik + Marcus have added engineering notes.

1) Option B committed minimum: we can structure a 6 GPU initial commitment for 6 weeks (pilot lane) with contractual ramp milestones to 25 GPUs at month 3 and 50 GPUs by month 6. That gives procurement a smaller near-term spend while preserving an enforceable ramp pathway. We can put ramp-based credits if milestones are met.

2) SLAs: For dedicated pools tied to an 18-month commitment (Option B) we offer a latency SLO of P99 <= 350ms for typical 1k token calls (on H100-equivalent). We will include an SLA clause for minimum allocation health and a credit schedule for sustained SLO misses. I'll ask legal to include explicit SLO definition language for inclusion in the term sheet.

3) Mixed GPU routing: Redwood will default to a profile-based routing policy — performance-critical routes pinned to H100-equivalent nodes, background/quantized workloads to A100-equivalent. Instance selection is automated by the serving runtime; engineers can override with route-level placement rules if you want deterministic placement.

Karthik, Marcus: any additional engineering caveats (warmups, pre-warming windows, and KV cache priming) to add?

Thanks,
Neha

> - GPU sizing: if your model is using retrieval-augmented generation with long context (>2k tokens), moving to H100s for the p99 path is important (memory + throughput). If context is shorter, A100 quantized variants yield much better cost per token.
> - Sequence-length assumptions in Neha's sheet drive cluster IOPS; please share sample traffic traces if you can.

Claire / team — throughput & warm-start sketches attached inline for quick sizing:

- Pilot lane (6 GPUs, H100-equivalent): ~1200 concurrent short-response calls (avg 600 tokens) with P95 latency ~180ms; sustained throughput ~20 tokens/sec/GPU for that profile.
- 25-GPU mid-point: can handle ~5k concurrent short-response calls with P95 ~220ms if KV cache hit-rate >70%.
- 50-GPU full scale: target for high concurrency batch with mixed-priority routing; expect linear-ish throughput with software-level batching but watch memory-bound model sizes which reduce per-GPU throughput.

Operational asks:
- We need a production data flow diagram for routing so SRE knows which routes are high-priority (pinned) vs low-priority (spill to quantized).
- A short 60-minute onboarding workshop for your infra team during week 1 of the pilot helps avoid startup misconfigurations.

I'll update the pro-forma with these throughput anchors and link into the XLSX.

Marcus Lin
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
